report:
**Conclusion: the claim is true.** High-quality randomized trial evidence shows that the two-dose adjuvanted recombinant zoster vaccine (RZV; Shingrix) substantially reduces shingles (herpes zoster) in immunocompetent adults aged 70 or older.

The pivotal phase 3 ZOE-70 placebo-controlled trial specifically enrolled this age group. It found vaccine efficacy against shingles of **91.3%** over roughly four years—meaning vaccinated participants had about a 91% lower *relative* risk than placebo recipients. The study also found reduced postherpetic neuralgia, a painful complication of shingles. This is especially meaningful because shingles risk and severity rise with age.  
https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1603800

Evidence did not end with the initial trial: follow-up of the pivotal ZOE-50/ZOE-70 cohorts found that protection and immune responses remained high through at least seven years after vaccination, supporting durable—not merely short-term—benefit.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34283213/

A systematic review/meta-analysis likewise characterizes trial efficacy in adults ≥70 as 91.3% against shingles (and 88.8% against postherpetic neuralgia), consistent with the pivotal trial.  
https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S2590136223001389

**Practical interpretation:** The evidence applies to completing the **two-dose** series; it does not mean zero risk, and trial efficacy may differ from real-world effectiveness. Still, the evidence is robust enough that CDC recommends two Shingrix doses for immunocompetent adults aged 50+ (including those ≥70), administered 2–6 months apart.  
https://www.cdc.gov/shingles/hcp/vaccine-considerations/index.html
